title: The homily
hookLine: the priest or deacon opens the readings for this crowd on this day
tomorrow: The Creed and the prayers of the faithful

cards: Ask people who grew up going to Mass about this part, and the stories come fast. The one who went on for forty minutes. The one who told the same joke every Easter.
And the one, maybe once, who said something that landed so exactly on someone's week that they wondered if somebody had told him.
It comes right after the Gospel, when the book has been kissed, the church settles back into the pews, and the priest or deacon begins to talk. Its name is older, and more interesting, than a speech.

teach.b: Homily comes from the Greek homilia: a conversation, a talk among people gathered together. Not a lecture from above. The verb shows up in a story you heard earlier on this path.
On the road to Emmaus, two disciples are walking home, talking together about everything that has happened, and in Luke's Greek, their talking shares the same root.
Then a stranger joins them and opens the scriptures to them. Later they say, in the Douay-Rheims: "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way, and opened to us the scriptures?"
That's what a homily is meant to do: take the readings everyone just heard and open them, for these people, on this day. Jesus did something like it in his hometown synagogue in Nazareth.
He stood, read a passage from Isaiah, sat down, and with every eye on him said: "This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears." Not a history lesson. Today.
So a homily isn't a sermon on just any topic.
The Church asks that it grow out of the readings and the Mass itself. It's given by a priest or deacon, and it's required on Sundays and holy days.

teach.h: WAS NOT OUR HEART BURNING WITHIN US?
teach.b: Pope Francis wrote pages on homilies, asking that they be short, warm, and more like a mother talking to her children than a lecture. Afterward, the Church suggests a short silence, so what was said can settle.
The word has been read; now it's handed to you, for this week.

how: After the Gospel, the congregation sits and the priest or deacon preaches the homily, drawn from the day's readings; it is required at Sunday and holy day Masses, and a short silence often follows.

games.q: you're Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth. you've just read a passage from Isaiah and sat down. every eye is on you. what do you say?
o: explain what Isaiah meant in his own time.
say that this scripture is fulfilled today, in their hearing.
ask someone else to explain it.
games.why: "This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears." not a history lesson: today. that's what a homily aims for.

practice: Think of the best sentence anyone ever said to you about life, from a pulpit, a classroom, a kitchen table, a friend at 2am; if nothing comes, take the one from Nazareth: this day is fulfilled.
Ask what it would mean for today, this ordinary Tuesday or whatever day it is. If you pray, you can ask for ears to hear.

wordCard.voice: Homily. From the Greek for conversation: the priest or deacon opening the day's readings for the people in front of him. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a conversation, a talk among a gathered group, the root of homily.

carryVoice: Your line: the word, for today. Old readings, opened for these people, this week. Until tomorrow.
